explain.say: In a crash a car can stop in about a tenth of a second, but your body keeps moving forward. An airbag puts a soft cushion in the way, and it has to be ready before you get there.

explain.say: Sensors called accelerometers feel how fast the car slows down. If the slowdown is far more sudden than any hard braking, the airbag computer decides to fire within a few hundredths of a second.

explain.say: The bag is full before you reach it. As you press in, gas escapes through vents, so it slows your head and chest gently over a longer time and a bigger area. Airbags work with seatbelts, not instead of them.

faq.q: How does an airbag know there has been a crash?
faq.a: Accelerometers in the car measure how quickly it slows down. Even hard braking is gentle compared with a crash, so only a sudden, violent slowdown triggers the airbag.
asks: Why doesn't an airbag go off when I brake hard?

faq.q: How fast does the airbag computer decide?
faq.a: Within a few hundredths of a second of the impact, the computer decides whether the crash is serious enough. If it is, it sends an electric signal to the inflator.
asks: How quickly does an airbag go off?

faq.a: An electric signal fires a small igniter in the inflator. It sets off a fast chemical reaction, or opens a can of compressed gas, producing harmless gas such as nitrogen or argon.
asks: What gas is in an airbag?

faq.q: How long does an airbag take to fill?
faq.a: An airbag fills in about 30 milliseconds, several times faster than a blink of an eye.
asks: How fast does an airbag inflate?

faq.q: Why does an airbag go down after it inflates?
faq.a: Vents let the gas out as your body presses into it. That way it soaks up your movement gently instead of bouncing you back. It is designed to work together with your seatbelt.

facts: A car airbag fills in about 30 milliseconds.
Airbags are designed to work with seatbelts, which hold you in the right place for the bag.
A rear-facing child seat must never be used in front of an active front airbag.
